Site-Selective sp
2
C−H Cyanation of Allenes via Copper-Catalyzed
Radical Relay
Zhongming Cheng,
∥
Tilong Yang,
∥
Can Li,
∥
Yunshun Deng, Fangjia Zhang, Pinhong Chen,
Zhenyang Lin,* Shengming Ma,* and Guosheng Liu*
Cite This: J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 25995−26002
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *

ABSTRACT: Compared with the extensively reported hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) at sp
3
C−H, abstraction of hydrogen atoms
at the sp
2
carbon is extremely rare. Here, we communicate the site-selective cyanation of the sp
2
C−H bond of allenes using the
strategy of copper-catalyzed radical relay. The reactions afford various allenyl nitriles directly from simple allenes with a broad
substrate scope and a remarkable functional group compatibility under mild conditions. These reactions exhibit excellent site-
selectivity toward sp
2
C−H, which can be attributed to the unique pocket created by the Cu-bound nitrogen-centered radical. The
favorable HAT on sp
2
C−H is due to crucial hydrogen bonding between the fluoride bonded to the Cu(II) center and the hydrogen
atom at the allylic position. These features enable the late-stage functionalization of druglike bioactive molecules containing an allene
motif.
A
llenes have been demonstrated as valuable building blocks
extensively utilized in the synthesis of diverse intricate
molecules.
1
The motifs are also found in natural products and
pharmaceuticals, thereby showcasing their significance in
biological systems.
2,3
For instance, because of their three-
dimensional structure, allenic scaffolds have been recognized as
the bioisosteres of propargylic compounds, furans, and
spirocyclobutanes, which exist in the nucleic acids, a class of
anti-HIV agents.
4
The allenic moiety in bioactive compounds
(e.g., allenic steroids and prostaglandins) often acts as the
reactive acceptor to inhibit the catalytic reactivity of enzymes
(Figure 1A).
3
Late-stage functionalization (LSF) of C−H bonds in
bioactive molecules has emerged as a powerful tool for the
advanced stages of their structural modification
5
to provide an
efficient approach to adjust their biological and pharmaco-
logical properties. Therefore, this streamlined synthetic process
of allene compounds would offer more efficient access to a
wide array of structurally diverse allene compounds compared
with the conventional synthetic approaches. However, very few
examples of allenyl C−H functionalization were reported
through the addition/elimination of C�C bonds
6
or Heck-
type allenyl C−H alkenylation.
7
The rare example of sp
2
C−H
alkenylation of allenes via palladium catalysis was reported by
Carreira and co-workers with a directing-group strategy,
8a
and
the elegant iron-catalzyed allenic C−H addition to imines and
aldehydes was reported by Wang and co-workers.
8b,c
There-
fore, the development of such general and practical methods is
quite urgent. Herein, we report a copper-catalyzed sp
2
C−H
cyanation of allenes where an uncommon site-selective
hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) on the sp
2
C−H was observed
as the key step, and the generated allenic sp
2
carbon radical
was regioselectively quenched by a copper(II) cyanide.
In the last several decades, the catalytic C−H activation has
garnered considerable attention from the scientific community
because of its remarkable efficiency and versatility in molecular
synthesis, and tremendous methods have been developed for
the efficient transformation of various C−H bonds.
9
Among
them, the methods involving hydrogen atom transfer (HAT)
have been recognized as an effective approach,
10
and the
reactions exclusively occurred to abstract sp
3
C−H bonds
(Figure 1B-i), whereas the sp
2
C−H bonds are always retained
(Figure 1B-ii).
11
Compared with the numerous studies on
functionalization of sp
3
C−H bonds, however, the function-
alization of the sp
2
C−H bond of allenes via HAT is not
documented. Instead, because of the inherent property of
cumulated diene, the reactions of allenes exclusively occur
through the π-bonds breaking (e.g., radical addition).
12
Not to
mention, multiple sp
2
allenic C−H bonds and active sp
3
allenylic C−H bonds often exist in the allene molecules
simultaneously. Therefore, the site-selective abstraction of the
hydrogen atom in sp
2
allenic or sp
3
allenylic positions becomes
a challenge. Meanwhile, after the HAT occurs either in a sp
2
or
sp
3
carbon center, the sequential regioselective functionaliza-
tion of the sp
2
allenic C-radical and its resonant sp
3
propargylic
C-radical (derived from sp
2
C−H), as well as the sp
3
allenylic
C-radical and its resonant sp
2
vinylic C-radical (derived from
sp
3
C−H), is another obstacle that results in the possible
functionalization products on the allenic,
13a−e
propargylic
13f−h
or vinylic positions (Figure 1C). A synthetically useful protocol
for the LSF of allene molecules would be needed to overcome
these challenges and limitations.

Inspired by our previous studies on sp
3
C−H functionaliza-
tion,
14
our initial survey focuses on the C−H cyanation of
allene 1a with CuOAc/Box as the catalyst, and electrophilic
fluorinating reagents (NF) were used as nitrogen-centered
radical (NCR) precursors. When the reaction was conducted
with 1 mol % copper catalyst (CuOAc/L1) in benzene, as
shown in Figure 2A, we were delighted to find that the direct
C−H cyanation of allene 1a, indeed, occurred via HAT rather
than a radical addition pathway. More importantly, apart from
our expected HAT on the allenylic sp
3
C−H at the C1 and C5
positions that delivered allenylic and vinylic cyanation products
2b−2e, surprisingly, an unexpected HAT on the sp
2
C−H
bonds occurred as a major reaction to deliver allenic nitrile
product 2a. We reasoned that the generated allenic carbon
radical could be stabilized by the coplanar π-orbital of the
adjacent C�C bond, which is attributed to the favorable
abstraction of hydrogen atom on the sp
2
C4-center. Moreover,
site-selectivity of HAT on the sp
2
allenic and sp
3
allenylic
position was relevant to the structure of NCR, where electron-
deficient N−F regents gave a higher preference for the
abstraction of hydrogen at sp
2
C−H (e.g., NF-3 > NF-2 > NF-
1), and the ratios of site-selectivity on allenic sp
2
C−H versus
allenylic sp
3
C−H ranged from 2.4 to 5.4 (red line). By further
changing the substituents on nitrogen from tert-butyl (NF-3)
to adamantyl (NF-4), the ratio could be further improved to
8.3. Moreover, the reaction in tert-butanol as the solvent gave a
better performance with a ratio of 12:1 so that the target
product 2a was obtained in 82% yield, along with the mixture
of 2b−2e in 7% yield. More importantly, further screening
revealed that the site-selectivity was significantly influenced by
the structure of ligands, whereas Box L2 with a gem-dibenzyl
group and bipyridine L3 gave poor site-selectivity (sp

when tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) was selected for the
radical cyanation of C−H bonds, where the free tert-butoxy
radical was recognized as a key species to carry out the HAT
process,
15
an even worse site-selectivity of HAT (sp
2

1.3:1) was observed, thereby indicating the unique reactivity of
NF-4 on the site-selective sp
2
C−H cyanation. A similar site-
selectivity of HAT (sp
2
/sp
3
= 1:1) was also obtained under
conditions of light-induced chain reaction where a free NCR
was generated from N−S reagent 3 (Figure 2B).
DFT calculations were conducted by using simple NF-3
along with L1, where the excellent selectivity (C
sp2
/C
sp3
= 9:1)
was still observed in
t
BuOH. As shown in Figure 2C, the DFT
results proved that the Cu(II)-bound NCR exhibits a higher
selectivity on the sp
2
over sp
3
C−H bonds than the free NCR.
Compared with abstracting hydrogen atom at C1 (TS_H
1
)
and C5 (TS_H
5
), an obvious hydrogen bonding interaction
(2.16 Å) was observed between the fluorine in the Cu(II)
center and the hydrogen atom at the allylic position of the
substrate, which results in the lower energy barrier of TS_H4,
thereby facilitating the highly site-selective HAT on the sp
2
C4
center.
With established reaction conditions, the substrate scope
was then investigated. As shown in Figure 3a, various tri-alkyl-
substituted allenes were demonstrated as the suitable
candidates for the radical cyanation of sp
2
C−H bonds.
Although the statistic number of hydrogen atoms on the sp
3
allenylic position is much higher (typically 6−8 times) than
that of sp
2
allenic positions, the reaction always afforded allenic
nitriles 5−8 with excellent site-selectivity (9:1 to 17:1) and

good yields (65−86%). More importantly, for the allene
substrate bearing extra benzylic C−H bonds, the reaction
occurred predominantly at the allenic position to provide
desired product 6 where the benzylic C−H was intact. Allenes
bearing synthestically versatile functionalities, such as imide,
hydroxy, carboxylate, and halide (e.g., Cl), in one allenic
position are suitable for the reaction to deliver products 9−12
with decent results. In addition, 1,1-disubstituted allene was
also suitable for the sp
2
C−H cyanation to deliver product 13
in 51% yield with good site-selectivity.
As shown in Figure 3b, we were delighted to find that aryl-
substituted allenes provided even better performance where an
excellent site-selectivity (typically C
sp
2
/C
sp
3
≈ 20:1) was
consistently observed in products 15−23. More importantly,
for the allene substrates bearing two types of allenic sp
2
C−H
bonds, the reactions also exhibited excellent site-selectivity. For
instance, the reaction of monosubstituted aryl−allene
proceeded smoothly to deliver 14 in 54% yield where the
HAT process only occurred to the allenic C1 position with
excellent site-selectivity. Moreover, 1,3-disubstituted aryl−
allenes were also identified as efficient substrates for the sp
2
C−H radical cyanation where the reactions also exclusively
occurred at C1 to give 15−17 in moderate yields with an
excellent site-selectivity (C1/C3 > 20:1). It should be
emphasized that for the allene substrates bearing an additional
sp
3
allylic C−H bond (23), the highly site-selective radical
cyanation of sp
2
C−H bond was also observed, where the
allylic C−H was intact. Finally, various heterocycles, such as
furan (24), thiophene (25), pyridine (26 and 28),
benzothiazole (27), and cyclic thioether (29) (Figure 3c) are
also compatible, which did not erode the site-selectivity of the
reactions.
Subsequently, the investigation was focused on complex
allene substrates derived from drug molecules and natural
products. As shown in Figure 3d, we were delighted to find
that a series of complex substrates derived from estrone (30),
glycine (31), cholesterol (32), nopol (33), ibuprofen (34),
pleuromulin (35), glycyrrhetinic acid (36), uridine (37) and
cholestanone (38) were suitable for this sp
2
radical cyanation
with excellent site-selectivity (typically sp
2
/sp
3
> 20:1), where
an array of functional groups, including ester, ether, amino
acids and sugar moieties, are compatible to the standard
conditions. Again, other active C−H bonds in benzylic (31,
36), allylic (32), and adjacent carbon positions of heteroatom
(30, 35−36, 38) were retained. In addition, the practical
application of our method in the laboratory was demonstrated
by the gram-scale preparations of compounds 32 and 38 with
excellent performance.
Allenyl nitriles have been recognized as important building
blocks for organic synthesis. For instance, compared with the
unactivated allenes, the lithiation of allenic nitrile 39 and the
subsequent 1,2-addition with benzaldehyde readily occurred to
give allenylic alcohol 40 in 92% yield; the D−A cyclization
reaction of 39 with furan also readily gave 41 under the copper
catalysis (Figure 4i). In addition, for the unprotected allenic
alcohol 38, the electrophilic brominating cyclization proceeded
very well to give 42 in 66% yield, in which the vinyl bromide
moiety allows for further cross coupling reactions (Figure 4ii).
Moreover, with the standard sp
2
C−H radical cyanation, the
generated product 44 could undergo the sequential oxidative
hydrolysis and copper-mediated cyclizative bromination to
provide 45 in 61% yield where the allene moiety could survive
under the oxidative conditions (Figure 4iii). Again, tetrasub-
stituted allenic nitrile 5 could be used for the synthesis of the

analogue of insect pheromone 46 via a sequential reduction of
the nitrile group with diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL)
and Wittig reaction (Figure 4iv). Finally, the nature of
electron-deficient allenyl nitrile allowed the interesting
asymmetric Lu’s [3 + 2] cyclization,
16
which yielded chiral
cyclopentenyl nitrile 48 in 75% yield and 86% ee where chiral
phosphine was employed as the organocatalyst (Figure
4iv).
17,18
Finally, the enantioselective cyanation of sp
2
C−H was also
investigated (Figure 5). With our previous catalytic system
Cu(I)/Box L4,
13b
the reactions of 1,3-disubstituted allenes 49
and 50 gave enantioselectivities of 88% and 92% ee,
respectively, although the asymmetric control on the sp
2
C−
H cyanation of trisubstituted allenes (51, 37% ee) needs
further attention.
In conclusion, a highly site-selective sp
2
C−H radical
cyanation of allenes has been established via a copper-catalyzed
radical relay. This method offers a streamlined approach for
the synthesis of multisubstituted allenic nitriles from simple
allenes with high efficiency. This catalytic system is also
suitable for the late-stage functionalization of allene-based
bioactive compounds
